messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Vignette:
Boun, a man of seventy-two with a gentle demeanor that suited his work as a nanny, described a life that had become a minefield of his own making. For the past eight months, since the night his husband, David, had hurt him, his world had shrunk to a series of carefully managed spaces. The main source of his distress, and what finally brought him to therapy, was an incident at work. He had been sitting on the floor with two-year-old Leo, stacking blocks, when the boy’s mother entered the room without a sound. Her sudden movement in his peripheral vision sent a jolt of pure terror through him. He gasped and scrambled backwards, knocking over the tower of blocks and making the child cry. The mother’s look of concerned confusion was, for Boun, a profound source of shame. He was certain that if he could not control these reactions, he would lose the job he loved, the only place he still felt competent.

The event itself remained a strange, detached film in his mind. He recalled the argument with David over finances, a familiar friction point, but that night it had felt different. David had been drinking. When Boun tried to walk away to let things cool down, David had followed him into the darkened bedroom, grabbing him and throwing him onto the bed. He remembered the weight of his husband pressing him down, the feeling of his arms being pinned, the darkness absolute except for the faint glow of a streetlamp through the window. When he recalls it now, it often feels as if it happened to someone else, another old man in a different life. But then a sensory detail will break through this wall of dissociation—the specific smell of whiskey on David’s breath or the rough texture of the duvet against his cheek—and the memory becomes terrifyingly immediate. The same raw terror he felt that night floods his body, and he finds his shoulders hunched forward, his arms pulled tight against his ribs, his body involuntarily re-enacting the posture of being held down.

This constant threat of re-experiencing the trauma has reshaped his daily existence. He has become a man who cannot tolerate darkness. At home, he insists on leaving lamps on in every room, even when he sleeps, a change that has created a silent, tense rift with David. At work, he makes sure every blind is open, every light switched on, explaining it away as being better for the children’s eyes. This vigilance is exhausting; he cannot remember the last time his body felt truly at rest. Even in the quiet moments when the children are napping and the house is still, he finds himself perched on the edge of the sofa, his muscles taut, listening for any unexpected sound. Relaxation feels like a dangerous indulgence he can no longer afford.

To prevent another conflict, Boun has adopted a policy of absolute agreeableness. He avoids any topic that might be stressful, both at home and at work. He preemptively soothes, placates, and agrees, no matter his own feelings. He is particularly vigilant about his own anger, which he has come to see as a profound danger. If he feels a flicker of frustration—at David’s carelessness, or a child’s tantrum—he smothers it instantly, convinced that expressing it could provoke another catastrophe. This self-imposed emotional straitjacket has left him feeling hollowed out, a polite and accommodating shell. Boun came to therapy not because he wanted to confront David, but because he could no longer bear the prison of his own nervous system. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, and his most fervent hope is to one day be able to sit in a quiet room and simply feel safe in his own skin again.
